The fastest way to find out whether a workflow pack works is to make it build its own marketing site. So that's what we did: the pages you're reading were designed, planned, and shipped through the waypower pipeline itself. This is the honest log of what that looked like.
documents.s: This site was built by the skills it documents

documents.t: "Build a docs site for the pack. New repo, a popular docs template, and use our own skills to do it." A vague brief — which is exactly the trigger condition for design-interview. It fired, and instead of scaffolding immediately, the agent asked. Two rounds: Register, users, purpose, outcome. Inferred hypotheses from the waypower repo (developers evaluating the pack in under five minutes; the install command as the success metric), confirmed and sharpened in conversation. Brand personality. Four candidate personalities; the pick was confident engineering — "Stripe/Vercel docs: the certainty of an expert who doesn't need noise." Plus the explicit anti-reference: AI-hype landing pages with gradient blobs and empty promises. The interview also settled the one architectural decision: Docusaurus — chosen for its built-in blog (this post needed somewhere to live), versioning that will track pack releases, and first-class GitHub Pages deployment.

The interview's output was committed to the repo before any page existed: PRODUCT.md — who the site serves, what success looks like, the five design principles ("show, don't tell", "the install command is sacred", "answer-first pages", "calm authority", "practice what you preach"). DESIGN.md — the seeded visual system: a pure-white surface, one deep marine-teal primary (seeded at OKLCH hue 200°) doing all the brand work, a saturated amber accent rationed to badges and the primary CTA, Inter + JetBrains Mono, near-zero motion. Every color on this site traces back to that file. The "no shadows, 1px borders" rule is why nothing here glows.
documents.s: The spec became artifacts before it became code

documents.t: Planning: the build was sliced into verifiable tickets — config, theme, content, landing, blog, deploy — each shippable on its own. Verification (completion-gate): "the site works" was not accepted until docusaurus build ran green and every internal link resolved — evidence, not assertion. Ship (finish-handoff): clean git history, pushed to a dedicated public repo, deployed to GitHub Pages, and this handoff of a blog post so the next session starts warm.
documents.s: Then the pipeline did what it does

documents.t: Two honest observations: The interview gate paid for itself immediately. The template question alone (Docusaurus vs VitePress vs Starlight vs MkDocs Material) would have been a coin flip without the interview's criteria: blog + versioning + Pages deploy made it a one-minute decision. The pipeline bends for content work. Strict RED-GREEN TDD doesn't map onto prose. The skills adapted — verification became "build passes, links resolve" — which is exactly what a good process should do: hold the discipline, flex the mechanics.

A workflow you wouldn't use on your own project is a workflow you shouldn't ship. This site is the proof artifact: the same pipeline documented in the skills reference produced the design system, the content, and the deploy — in one session, with the gates doing their job. Try it on yours: npx skills add mohmaedeslam00116/waypower --all -g --copy

Your agent already knows how to code. The bottleneck was never the model's syntax — it's that nobody taught it how to work: how to refuse a vague brief, how to plan before building, how to prove a claim before making it. waypower v0.1.0 is out today: 13 pressure-tested agent skills forming one idea-to-ship pipeline for Claude Code and compatible harnesses. npx skills add mohmaedeslam00116/waypower --all -g --copy

1 orchestrator — using-waypower, always active, routes every task to the right process skill and disarms the rationalizations agents use to skip process. 8 process skills — auto-invoked on their triggers: design-interview, tracer-plan, seam-design, seam-driven-tdd, hypothesis-debugging, domain-glossary, completion-gate, dual-axis-review. 4 tool skills — invoked by name when you want them: waymap, finish-handoff, deep-research, authoring-skills.

Every skill was graded against paired baseline runs — the same pressure scenario executed with and without the skill. 12 of 13 discriminate cleanly: agents with the skill demonstrably behave differently than agents without it. The thirteenth (domain-glossary) is documented honestly and being hardened for the next release. The eval scenarios ship inside the pack (evals/evals.json per skill), so you can re-run the evidence yourself instead of taking our word for it.
Getting started — five minutes to your first pipeline session The pipeline — the six stages and where you stay in the loop Skills reference — all 13 in detail GitHub · skills.sh
Claude Code or a compatible agent harness that supports skills (Cursor, Cline, Codex CLI…) Node.js 18+ (only for the npx installer)

The recommended path — all 13 skills, global, copied (not symlinked): npx skills add mohmaedeslam00116/waypower --all -g --copy Pick a single skill instead by naming it: npx skills add mohmaedeslam00116/waypower --skill seam-driven-tdd -g --copy The installer runs a security audit on the pack before copying (waypower passes: Safe, 0 alerts, Low Risk).

The skills should now exist in your global skills directory: ls ~/.claude/skills You should see using-waypower, design-interview, tracer-plan, seam-design, seam-driven-tdd, hypothesis-debugging, domain-glossary, completion-gate, dual-axis-review, waymap, finish-handoff, deep-research, authoring-skills.

Open a session in your harness, in any repo, and describe a feature you want: Claude Code Cursor Cline Codex CLI claude Then, in the session: "I want to add rate limiting to the API." Open the Agent chat (Ctrl/Cmd + I) in your repo, then: "I want to add rate limiting to the API." Open the Cline panel in VS Code, then: "I want to add rate limiting to the API." codex Then, in the session: "I want to add rate limiting to the API." Whichever harness you use, this is what should happen next — without you asking for any of it: using-waypower (always active) classifies the request as creative work and routes it. design-interview fires and asks you frontier questions instead of guessing — it will not let the agent write code from a vague brief. It ends at a written spec you approve. Only then does implementation begin. tracer-plan slices the spec into tickets; seam-driven-tdd implements them test-first, red before green. Before "done" is claimed, completion-gate demands the verification commands actually ran — and dual-axis-review sends two review agents over the diff. finish-handoff merges, cleans up, and writes a handoff note for the next session. If step 2 didn't happen and the agent jumped straight to code, the skills aren't loading — check the install directory and restart the session.

The four tool skills never auto-fire. Ask for them explicitly: "waymap this" — chart a huge effort into decision tickets "deep-research: how does X's API handle Y?" — primary-source research, findings committed to the repo "finish-handoff" — integrate and hand off completed work "authoring-skills" — write or harden a skill of your own
Re-run the same install command — it overwrites the copies with the latest release: npx skills add mohmaedeslam00116/waypower --all -g --copy -y
Delete the skill directories from ~/.claude/skills/ (and any other agent directories the installer detected).

Your agent already knows how to code. waypower teaches it how to work. waypower is a pack of 13 agent skills that install into Claude Code (or any compatible agent harness) and give it a complete, disciplined workflow — from the first vague idea to a shipped, reviewed branch. One orchestrator skill is always active; it routes every task through the right process skill at the right moment, with you approving the decisions that matter. npx skills add mohmaedeslam00116/waypower --all -g --copy

waypower is not a bag of tricks — it's one pipeline: idea ──► design-interview ──► spec ──► tracer-plan ──► seam-driven-tdd ──► review ──► finish-handoff ▲ you approve tickets red → green dual-axis merge + handoff For efforts too big for one session, waymap charts the fog into decision tickets first. For anything, completion-gate makes "done" mean verified.

Kind Count How they run Examples Orchestrator 1 Always active — enforces the pipeline using-waypower Process 8 Auto-invoked when their trigger matches design-interview, seam-driven-tdd Tool 4 You invoke by name, when you want them waymap, deep-research

Every skill ships with its own eval scenarios (evals/evals.json) and was graded against paired baseline runs — the same task, with and without the skill. 12 of 13 skills discriminate cleanly (the thirteenth, domain-glossary, is being hardened for the next release). The failures were fixed before release, not documented after.
This documentation site was itself built through the waypower pipeline — design-interviewed, planned, and shipped with the skills it documents. Read how →
Getting started — install and first session in 5 minutes The pipeline — the full idea-to-ship flow, stage by stage Skills reference — all 13 skills in detail

waypower treats every task as a journey through six stages. Each stage has one skill that owns it, and human-in-the-loop gates where the agent must stop and get your approval before proceeding. 01INTAKE 02DESIGN 03PLAN 04BUILD 05VERIFY 06SHIP GATE / 02design-interview “What are we really building?” Frontier interview rounds end at a written spec that you approve. This gate is the cheapest place in the entire pipeline to change your mind. Six stages, six gates. Click a stage to inspect it — who owns it, what it asks, and where you stay in control.
Always active. Classifies every incoming request, fires the right process skill, and enforces the red-flag rules ("this is too small for a process" is usually the moment the process matters most).

No code from a vague brief. The skill interviews you in frontier rounds until the design is fully formed, then produces a written spec. You approve it before anything is built. This gate is the cheapest place in the entire pipeline to change your mind.

The approved spec becomes tracer-bullet tickets: thin, end-to-end slices that each leave the system working. Executed with per-task review. Too big for one session? Invoke waymap first — it charts the fog into decision tickets on your issue tracker and resolves them one at a time.

Test-first at user-confirmed seams. The Iron Law: no production code without a failing test; RED is verified before GREEN is written. seam-design supplies the shared deep-module vocabulary whenever an interface is being shaped. Bug mid-flight? hypothesis-debugging takes over: ranked, falsifiable hypotheses — never guess-and-check.

completion-gate: no success claim without the verification commands having actually run — evidence before assertions, always. Then dual-axis-review dispatches two parallel review agents over the diff (Standards + Spec) before merge.
Integrate (merge / PR / keep branch), clean the workspace, and compact the session into a handoff note the next agent — or next you — can pick up cold.

Gate You decide Spec approval What gets built Ticket approval How it gets sliced Seam confirmation Where the interfaces are Merge When it ships Everything between gates runs autonomously — that's the deal: the agent earns your trust at the gates so it can run fast between them.
documents.s: Where you stay in the loop

documents.t: SKILL / 13toolon-call TRIGGER Creating or hardening a skill of your own OUTPUT A pressure-tested skill with its own evals PAIRS WITH using-waypower One line: the meta-skill — how waypower's own skills were built, packaged so you can build yours the same way.
Ask for it by name when creating a new skill, editing an existing one, or verifying a skill works before deploying it.

Applies test-driven development to process documentation: RED — write pressure scenarios and run them without the skill. Watch the agent fail (or succeed — which tells you the skill isn't needed). GREEN — write the minimal skill that changes the behavior. REFACTOR — close the loopholes: the rationalizations agents used to skip the skill, named and disarmed in the text itself. Plus the mechanics: frontmatter that triggers reliably, invocation rules, file structure, and the paired-eval grading waypower itself was gated on.

Skills that provably change behavior — not prompt-flavored wishful thinking. Every waypower skill on this site passed exactly this process (12 of 13 discriminate cleanly; the thirteenth is honest about it).
The release discipline behind all 13 skills; its output plugs straight into using-waypower's routing.

SKILL / 08processauto-invoked TRIGGER "Done" is about to be claimed OUTPUT Evidence — the verification commands actually ran and passed PAIRS WITH dual-axis-reviewfinish-handoff One line: "done" now means verified — the agent cannot claim success it hasn't demonstrated.
Whenever the agent is about to claim work is complete, fixed, or passing — before commits, PRs, or closing tickets.

Requires the verification commands to actually run (tests, build, lint, typecheck — whatever proves the claim) and their output to be inspected. Blocks success claims made from memory, assumption, or "it passed a minute ago". Makes failures visible instead of summarizing them away.
You can trust the word "done". When a waypower-driven agent says the tests pass, they passed — in this session, just now, with output to show for it.
The last gate before dual-axis-review; every skill that produces work answers to it.

SKILL / 12toolon-call TRIGGER "deep-research: <question>" — facts that need primary sources OUTPUT A cited answer, committed to your repo as Markdown PAIRS WITH domain-glossary One line: give a question to a background agent that reads the primary sources — and commits what it found to your repo.

Ask for it by name: "deep-research: how does X handle Y?" Use it for API facts, library internals, protocol behavior — anywhere the answer should come from documentation and source, not from model memory.

Investigates against high-trust primary sources: official docs, source code, RFCs — not blog summaries of blog summaries. Runs as a background agent, so your main session keeps moving. Captures findings as a Markdown file in the repo — the research becomes project knowledge, citable and reviewable, not chat ephemera.
Answers you'd stake a design on, with the sources attached — and a research trail the next person (or agent) can extend instead of redoing.
Feeds design-interview when the fog is factual; research tickets in waymap are exactly its job.

SKILL / 02processauto-invoked TRIGGER A vague or high-stakes creative brief OUTPUT A written spec you approve before any code exists PAIRS WITH tracer-plandual-axis-review One line: no code from a vague brief — the agent interviews you until the design is fully formed, then stops at your approval gate.
Before any creative work: creating features, building components, adding functionality, modifying behavior. It's the mandatory first step of the pipeline.

Classifies the request — spike, bounded, or architectural — which sets how deep the interview goes. Interviews in frontier rounds: each round pushes the boundary of what's still undecided (users, data, failure modes, boundaries) instead of asking laundry-list questions. Ends at a written spec — and waits. Implementation cannot start until you approve it.

A spec you actually read and signed off on — which means no "that's not what I meant" three hours later. The interview surfaces the questions you didn't know needed answering while they're still free to answer.

You: add caching to the dashboard Agent (design-interview): Before I touch code — three rounds of questions. Round 1: what reads hurt today — first paint, or interactions after? Who notices: you, or users? What's the staleness budget — seconds, minutes?
Hands its approved spec to tracer-plan. For efforts too foggy for a single spec, route through waymap first.

SKILL / 07processauto-invoked TRIGGER A concept gets named, or an ADR is written OUTPUT One word per concept — CONTEXT.md and ADRs stay coherent PAIRS WITH design-interview One line: the project's vocabulary police — one name per concept, kept in a living CONTEXT.md, so agents and humans stop talking past each other.
When discussing codebase terminology, writing or editing a CONTEXT.md, or recording or editing an ADR (architecture decision record).

Builds and sharpens the domain model: entities, relationships, and the exact word for each concept. Owns the CONTEXT.md glossary — the single source of truth an agent reads to learn what things are called in this repo. Records decisions as ADRs so "why" survives the people who made it.

Agents that use your project's real vocabulary from message one — and never invent a second name for a concept that already has one. :::note Known limitation domain-glossary is the one skill whose evals didn't discriminate cleanly at v0.1.0 — it's being hardened for the next release. It works; we just haven't proven how much yet. :::
Feeds vocabulary into every other skill; its glossary is most valuable to design-interview and seam-design.

SKILL / 09processauto-invoked TRIGGER A diff is ready — or review feedback arrives OUTPUT Two parallel verdicts: engineering standards and spec fitness PAIRS WITH completion-gatefinish-handoff One line: every diff gets reviewed twice, in parallel — once against engineering standards, once against the spec it claims to implement.
When a task, ticket, or feature is complete and before merging — and again when review feedback arrives, to verify comments before implementing them.

Dispatches two review sub-agents over the diff: Standards axis — code quality, conventions, security, error handling, the things that are always true. Spec axis — does this diff actually do what the approved spec said? Nothing more, nothing less — the axis that catches "works, but wrong thing". Feedback arriving from humans gets the same treatment: verified before it's implemented, so a mistaken review comment doesn't get obediently merged.
Pre-merge review that catches the two failure modes that matter — bad code, and good code for the wrong requirement — without you reading every line.
Runs after completion-gate, before finish-handoff merges.

SKILL / 11toolon-call TRIGGER "finish-handoff" — work is complete and verified OUTPUT A clean merge and a warm handoff note PAIRS WITH completion-gate One line: the landing sequence — merge, clean up, and leave a handoff note good enough that the next session starts warm, not cold.
Ask for it by name when implementation is complete and verified. Also the bridge for detours: hand off out to a prototype session, hand what you learned back to the main thread.

Integrates the work — merge, pull request, or deliberately keep the branch, your call. Cleans the workspace — no orphaned branches, no stray state. Compacts the session into a handoff: what was decided, what was built, what's verified, what's next, and where the bodies are buried.
Sessions that compose. Work from three weeks ago resumes in minutes because the handoff note carries the context the chat history no longer does.
The final stage of the pipeline; the natural companion of waymap for multi-session efforts.

SKILL / 06processauto-invoked TRIGGER A bug or failure with an unknown cause OUTPUT Ranked falsifiable hypotheses, each tested by the cheapest experiment PAIRS WITH seam-driven-tddcompletion-gate One line: debugging as the scientific method — ranked hypotheses, each falsifiable, each tested by the cheapest experiment that could kill it.
On any bug, test failure, or unexpected behavior — before any fix is proposed. It has pipeline priority: a bug found mid-implementation pauses seam-driven-tdd until the root cause is known.

Ranks hypotheses by likelihood × cost of testing. Falsifies, doesn't confirm — each experiment is designed to kill a hypothesis, not to make the favorite look right. Tight feedback loop — smallest possible reproduction, one variable at a time. Only then: a fix, verified against the reproduction — which usually becomes the regression test.
Fixes that stay fixed. No "try this and see" loops, no whack-a-mole — and a written trail of what was ruled out, so the next occurrence starts from evidence, not folklore.
Its regression tests land through seam-driven-tdd; verified fixes pass completion-gate before being called done.

SKILL / 04processauto-invoked TRIGGER An interface or module seam is being shaped OUTPUT Deep-module contracts before implementation PAIRS WITH seam-driven-tdd One line: the design vocabulary every other skill speaks — deep modules, well-placed seams, interfaces worth testing at.
When designing or improving a module's interface, finding deepening opportunities, deciding where a seam goes, making code more testable or AI-navigable — or when another skill needs the vocabulary.

Applies deep-module thinking: small interface, large implementation. Flags shallow modules that leak their insides. Locates seams — the boundaries where behavior can be observed and verified — so tests have somewhere honest to live. Keeps interfaces AI-navigable: an agent can find the right seam without reading the whole codebase, which is what makes the rest of the pipeline fast.
Modules an agent (and a human) can safely change. The seams you confirm here are exactly where seam-driven-tdd writes its tests.
The design half of seam-driven-tdd; used throughout tracer-plan execution whenever a new interface appears.

SKILL / 05processauto-invoked TRIGGER Implementation begins at confirmed seams OUTPUT Verified RED before every GREEN — enforced, not suggested PAIRS WITH seam-designcompletion-gate One line: test-first development where tests live at seams you confirmed — with the discipline enforced, not suggested.
When implementing any feature, bugfix, or behavior change — before writing implementation code.

The Iron Law: no production code without a failing test that demands it. Mandatory verify-RED: the agent must watch the new test fail for the right reason before writing the implementation. A test that never failed proves nothing. Tracer-bullet slicing: behavior lands in thin, end-to-end increments (inherited from tracer-plan), each green before the next begins. Tests sit at user-confirmed seams (see seam-design) — so they survive refactors instead of punishing them.
A test suite that documents behavior at the boundaries that matter, and an agent that cannot quietly skip the red phase — the most common way "TDD" degenerates into writing tests after the fact.
Design vocabulary from seam-design; bugs found mid-cycle escalate to hypothesis-debugging; completion claims pass through completion-gate.

SKILL / 03processauto-invoked TRIGGER An approved spec for a multi-step task OUTPUT Tracer-bullet tickets — thin slices that each leave the system working PAIRS WITH seam-driven-tddwaymap One line: the spec becomes thin end-to-end slices — each one leaves the system working — instead of one big-bang implementation.
When you have an approved spec (from design-interview) for a multi-step task — before any code is touched.

Slices the spec into tracer-bullet tickets: the thinnest path through all layers that delivers observable behavior, first. Sequences the remaining tickets behind it, each independently verifiable. Executes with per-task review — drift is caught at ticket boundaries, not at the end.
Working software from ticket one. If priorities change mid-build, what's already merged still works — you never hold a half-built "big plan".
Receives specs from design-interview; hands each ticket to seam-driven-tdd for test-first implementation.

SKILL / 01orchestratoralways active TRIGGER Every incoming task — before anything else is allowed to start OUTPUT The right skill, routed — with the red-flag rules enforced PAIRS WITH design-interviewcompletion-gate One line: the traffic controller — it decides which process skill owns whatever you just asked for, and it doesn't let the agent skip.
Always. It loads at the start of every conversation and stays active for the whole session.

Establishes the mandatory skill-invocation rule: when a task matches a process skill's trigger, that skill runs — no exceptions for "small" tasks. Maintains the priority ladder for conflicting triggers (e.g. a bug found mid-implementation routes to hypothesis-debugging before seam-driven-tdd resumes). Names the red flags — the rationalizations agents use to skip process ("I'll just quickly…", "this is trivial, no need for…") — and overrides them. Exempts the four tool skills from auto-invocation: they run only when you call them by name.
A session where the pipeline is the default, not the exception. You never have to remember which skill exists — the orchestrator routes; you decide at the gates.
Everything. It's the reason the other eight process skills fire at all.

SKILL / 10toolon-call TRIGGER "waymap this" — an effort too big to see whole OUTPUT A decision map of tickets, resolved one at a time PAIRS WITH tracer-plan One line: for work too big for one session — a living map of decision tickets on your issue tracker, resolved one at a time until the way is clear.

Ask for it by name: "waymap this." Use it when the effort is large and the path is foggy — a migration, a new product area, anything where "just start" would mean discovering the plan by accident. Never auto-fires.

Chart mode: names the destination first (via design-interview), then maps the frontier breadth-first into a single map issue (waymap:map) plus child tickets. Ticket types: research (find out), prototype (try it cheap), grilling (decide with a human), task (build it) — each carrying a waymap:<type> label. Blocking edges wire the dependency graph, so the map always shows what's resolvable now. Resolve mode: clears one ticket at a time; the map is an index, not a knowledge store — findings live in the tickets.
The fog made visible and finite. At any moment you can answer: where are we, what's decided, what's blocking what, what's next — across sessions, agents, and weeks.
Feeding resolved tickets into tracer-plan and seam-driven-tdd; session continuity via finish-handoff.
